query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high-energy ball milling (mechanical alloying) process to W and Cu powders, followed by optimized spark-plasma sintering (SPS) with controlled atmosphere and temperature ramp, will yield a W–Cu composite with significantly reduced void fraction and improved interfacial contact, resulting in higher thermal conductivity and mechanical durability compared to conventional infiltration or powder sintering methods.
generation.material_initial_state: W and Cu powders (particle sizes <10 μm), mixed in desired volume ratio for fusion-reactor joint application.
generation.intervention: High-energy ball milling of W and Cu powders to achieve nanostructured mixing, followed by spark-plasma sintering under controlled atmosphere (inert gas or vacuum) and optimized temperature ramp (below Cu boiling, above Cu melting, below W melting).
generation.conditions: Processing: SPS at 900–1100 °C, pressure 50–100 MPa, dwell time 5–30 min, inert atmosphere. Service: Thermal cycling and neutron irradiation as in fusion-reactor joint conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanostructured W–Cu interface with minimal voids and high interfacial contact area.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical alloying breaks up oxide films and promotes intimate mixing; SPS rapidly consolidates powders, minimizing grain growth and void formation, yielding a dense composite with enhanced thermal pathways and mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thermal conductivity and mechanical durability (e.g., flexural strength, toughness) will be at least 20% higher than baseline W skeleton filled with molten Cu or conventionally sintered W–Cu composites, with void fraction <2%.
generation.baseline: W skeleton filled with molten Cu (infiltration) or conventionally sintered W–Cu composite.
generation.boundary: Processing temperature must remain below Cu boiling and W melting; powder purity and atmosphere must be controlled; service conditions limited to fusion-reactor joint thermal and irradiation loads.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of improvement depends on powder quality, milling parameters, and SPS optimization; possible trade-off between grain refinement and mechanical toughness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare W–Cu composites by (a) conventional infiltration, (b) conventional powder sintering, and (c) high-energy ball milling + SPS. Characterize void fraction (via X-ray tomography), interfacial contact (via SEM/EDS), thermal conductivity (laser flash), and mechanical durability (flexural strength, toughness tests).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ball-milled + SPS composite does not show at least 20% higher thermal conductivity and mechanical durability, or void fraction <2% compared to baseline methods, the hypothesis is falsified.
